item.title: Osi Umenyiora on the journey that led to NFL Africa
item.dc:creator: Mary Omatiga
item.description: Osi Umenyiora reflects on the unlikely path that inspired NFL Africa.
item.content:encoded:
Umenyiora on how Nigerian culture has shaped life
Osi Umenyiora joins By Way of Africa to discuss growing up in Nigeria, how Nigerian culture and values have shaped him, and the importance of giving back.

Born in London and spending his formative years in Nigeria, Osi Umenyiora had never even heard of American football until he moved to the U.S. as a teenager.

After moving to Auburn, Alabama, he took up the sport in high school and eventually earned an opportunity at Troy University. He was drafted by the New York Giants in 2003 and went on to win Super Bowls XLII and XLVI.

Umenyiora spent ten years with the Giants and two seasons with the Atlanta Falcons before retiring in 2015.

The rest, as they say, is history. Yet Umenyiora's story was far from over.

"My whole story has just been one of pure fortune, and so I looked at it like, 'Okay, I've been given this opportunity, and now I'm working with the NFL. How can I now give this opportunity to more people?'"

That's where an e-mail to NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell snowballed into NFL Africa, the league's initiative to grow the game on the continent and perhaps Umenyiora's most impactful chapter yet.

In the conversation below, part of NBC Sports' By Way of Africa series, Umenyiora reflects on his childhood in Nigeria, the story behind NFL Africa's creation, and what the initiative's growth means to him.

*This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Mary Omatiga: Osi, you were born in London, but I read that you lived in Nigeria from age 7 to 14. What memories come to mind when you think of your childhood there?

Osi Umenyiora: Nigeria to me is a very special place. It's a place that I hope to one day return to and live. Growing up there meant so much to me. My family being there, coming back there. Because of the way we were raised — and we were raised in a very Nigerian way — when I got there, the only difference really was the climate. Other than that, it was basically the same things going on. But overall, it was just a really, really great experience and time in my life. It's something that I'll never forget and something that I cherish.

How did that time there shape you into who you are today?

Umenyiora: In a multitude of ways. The environment there teaches you how to survive first and foremost. It instills toughness. There are so many things that you see there that, whenever you leave that environment, the ability to thrive in those situations, you can carry them with you pretty much anywhere.

I know they say that if you can make it in New York, you can make it anywhere, but really, it's if you can make it in Lagos, Nigeria, you can pretty much make it anywhere.

Names can carry so much weight in African culture. What’s your full Nigerian name and what does it translate to?

Umenyiora: Ogemdi Ositadinma Iloabuchi Umenyiora.

My father would actually name us after periods in his life. So Ogemdi means 'My time is now'. Ositadinma means, 'From today, things will be good', and Iloabuchi basically means, 'The heart of who is God'. So it's three different names.

Then one of [my dad's] friends went to him and was like, 'You have four sons at this point, and none of them are named after you. Why don't you name one of your sons after you?'

So he just started calling me Osi randomly when I was two years old and that's how I got the name. But my first name is actually Ogemdi.

How do you think the meaning of your name has played out in your life?

Umenyiora: First and foremost, just understanding that my father would name all his children — and he had ten of them — after different periods of his life. I think it was a very special and sentimental thing for us because a lot of times you don't really know the meaning of your names, or people just randomly call their children whatever.

But the fact that my father took the time to think about each one of his children and specifically name us after something that happened translates, and it just gives your name that much more pride and that much more meaning.

Also, the thing about Nigerian names is you can tell where somebody's from within Nigeria just by hearing their name, which is kind of unique to a lot of people. So I can hear somebody's name, and I'll be like, 'Okay, this guy is Fulani, or he's Hausa, Yoruba, or Igbo, simply by hearing their name.

The name really is an identifier. It's a marker of who you are, where you come from, and a lot of times it actually carries your whole family history with you.

You are Igbo. Can you talk about the values and traditions that come from your culture that have led to your success on and off the field?

Umenyiora: Being from the Igbo tribe, we're very, very proud people. Obviously, there was a situation back in the '60s and '70s where Nigeria fought a war. Biafra was trying to secede from Nigeria. It didn't work out well, but the Igbo people were the main people who were in that. So, just being a part of that tribe, I would say I find it interesting how I don't really consider myself Igbo until I get to Nigeria.

Because outside of Nigeria, you're just Nigerian. Everybody is cool. They're family. You're just one. But the minute you go back into Nigeria, that's when you become either Igbo, Hausa, Yoruba, Fulani, Ijaw, Efik, Ibibio — one of those tribes.

To be honest, I wish that we would take more of the approach that we have outside of Nigeria into Nigeria, so we can be more cohesive and really move as one within the country. Because outside of the country, my best friends are Yoruba, Hausa, it doesn't really matter until you go back in. I wish we would stop that.

You are a two-time Super Bowl champion, a New York Giants legend. So much of your journey was shaped by hard work and values, but your journey is also a testament to the power of having someone believe in you and take a chance on you.

How has that inspired this chapter of your life as the lead for NFL Africa?

Umenyiora: Oh, massively! A lot of times, people can look at things that they do and things that they accomplish and think that they're the ones who did it. For me, I've never thought that way.

I always knew that I was very fortunate. I was lucky to have the parents that I did who were able to send me to America. I was lucky to be able to start playing the game of football, which gave me the opportunity to get a scholarship and then go on to the NFL.

My whole story has just been one of pure fortune, and so I looked at it like, 'Okay, I've been given this opportunity, and now I'm working with the NFL. How can I now give this opportunity to more people?'

Because there are so many people, especially when I was growing up, who were more talented than me, had much more ability than me, but they just didn't have the parents, or they didn't have the [opportunities]. So now that I'm in a position to help, why would I not try to put those people in the exact same position that I'm in? As opposed to just going back there and doing the regular things.

'Oh, we're going to do a charity here. We're going to do this and that.'

Cool. I get all that, but for me, it was about this: There are tremendous athletes there. There are people there with real ability, and all they need is just a pathway. All they need is just somebody to hold the door open for them, so they can come and make the best of their abilities.

For me, the idea that I had this opportunity to do something like that, given the fact that I was given that exact same opportunity, was monumental, and it's something that I knew that I had to do.

It's been brewing for 20 years. I know people see what's going on now, but this is something that has been a long journey, a long process, and is just now starting to come to fruition.

Tell me about the e-mail you sent to Roger Goodell that started that long process.

Umenyiora: Roger is my guy. We spent quite a bit of time together, and so, just the understanding of the NFL trying to expand internationally, I've been in the UK, doing that work. But if you look at the actual rosters in the NFL, you hear a lot of African names. It wasn't like that when I came in. There were just a couple, and now if you look, there are over a hundred.

You can't have all these international games and try to expand into all these international markets, but the place where most of your players are coming from internationally, you don't have a division, or you don't have anything that you're doing there. I think that wasn't right, and so I had the conversation with him. I sent him the email, and in all fairness to him, he didn't even hesitate.

As soon as I sent him the email, he saw the vision immediately and was like, 'Hey, go do this. Let's get this done.'

So kudos to him for that.

Since then, you’ve led camps in Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, and Egypt. What does the growth of NFL Africa mean to you?

Umenyiora: It's amazing. I think when I go there and I see how many people are playing the sport, especially flag football, they're taking to it. It's growing tremendously, and people understand the game. They're adopting the culture. They love it. They know the players.

It's really so crazy because when I left Nigeria, that wasn't even a thought. I had never even heard of American football. There wasn't even an inkling that something like this existed until I got to America.

So now, to go back there and see that people know the NFL, people know the players, they're doing the dances — it's really a testament to all the hard work that we've done and that we will continue to do. I'm really excited about it!

What are you most proud of?

Umenyiora: Well, I think what I'm going to be most proud of hasn't happened yet. The scouts are sending you videos of a lot of these guys, and you see them, and they don't have the body types. They're big, but they're not like American football big.

So you go there, you do the first camp. You see them. You train them. You talk to them. They're excited. And then we come down there. We have the NFL Africa camp. Then, literally within like a couple of months, you see them in America, in college or in the NFL.

I can never get over that feeling because I know where I saw them first, and I know what's going on on the ground there. I know the struggles that they're enduring, and then literally within a couple of months you see them on NFL rosters or going to big-time colleges, and you're like, 'This is crazy.'

Just seeing that process repeat itself, and knowing that I had this idea — that this was possible because of something that I had done. Having the vision, and then all of a sudden seeing it come to reality is something that I wish everybody could experience.

I wish you could see some of the guys and the places that they’re training, and then the next thing you know, you see them at the NFL Africa camp, and then within a couple of months, you look up, they're playing for the Baltimore Ravens.

It's a really special thing to experience and I'm excited to keep it going.

You've gone to these camps, and you’ve actually had the opportunity to bring NFL players with you. Some of them are actually experiencing Africa for the very first time.

What has that experience been like for you to see people experience the culture for the first time?

Umenyiora: Amazing! There's really nothing like it. A lot will have African names because of their parents. They are first-generation, so they've never been. They've been raised in African households, so they've been hearing all the stories, getting a little understanding of it, and then to see them experience it for the first time and be like, 'Wow, I'm really from here. My parents are from here.'

It's mind-blowing, and they never forget it. It's something that stays with them and lives with them. They want to give back. They want to keep going. And some of them, the minute that happens to them, there's like a light bulb switch in their head, and they're like, 'Okay, what can I do now? How can I help? How can I be of service?'

It's really cool to bring that experience to people who have never experienced it. Even some Americans have been there, and they see it, and it [resonates] with them because you just see a whole bunch of people who look exactly like you.

It's just being in that environment and knowing that these are your roots. I think it's something everybody really should experience.

Have there been any moments or reactions from players that have stayed with you?

Umenyiora: I think when we went to Ghana, and we went to Cape Coast Castle, that was crazy, to see their reactions and how they absorbed the reality of what their ancestors went through. That was a tough day, to be honest. So I would say that one stood out with me for sure.

NFL Africa shared on Instagram recently that this season there are 24 African countries represented in the league. Players are representing; they are coming to game day in their traditional attire. They are giving back to the continent, hosting camps and foundations.

What does it mean to you to see so many players representing with pride and giving back?

Umenyiora: It's amazing, right? When you see it, you're like, 'Man, this is absolutely crazy.' Because it wasn't like that before. There was a time when you almost had to hide your identity in a way. So the fact that there are so many people who are so proud of where they come from and their heritage, I think it's also a testament to Africa in general and some of the strides that Africa has made.

Now people want to be associated with something that they see as being good. It's amazing to see them wear their colors with pride. If you look at the back of the NFL helmets, they'll have the American flag, and then they'll have whatever country they're from.

But I think those things are tremendous, not only for Africa itself or the countries, but also for America to really be a unifier and bring people and cultures together so they can understand where they're from.

You’ve witnessed the growth of NFL internationally, with games taking place all over the world. What do you think it would be like for people to actually experience an NFL game on the continent?

Umenyiora: I think that would be incredible. Baby steps, though. There are a couple of things that we need to get sorted out and make sure that we have our own houses in order to make sure we're capable of hosting an NFL game on the African continent.

I think there are some countries there that are really making incredible strides, and they're doing things with their stadiums, facilities, and with their infrastructure to make sure that something like that can happen. But I'm pretty sure at some point in the future it's going to happen.

Before then, I think we need to build a league of our own on the continent. That's really where my mind is. We need to focus on building something that captures the value on the continent itself, and actually develops people, trains them, and allows them to keep some of that talent there in Africa and provide entertainment for the people there.

That's the next step, and I think that's where we're going to be next.

You’re also a flag football ambassador. The sport will make its Olympic debut at the 2028 Games in Los Angeles. What do you hope to see from African nations?

Umenyiora: There's no question, in my mind anyway, that the African athlete is probably the best athlete in the world. They're just untrained. So all we have to do is give them the opportunities, the tools, and all the training necessary, and I think this is a sport that they're going to dominate.

I think we're probably a little far behind in terms of the training and getting the players where they need to be in terms of their physical ability, their [knowledge of the game]. But in short order, I think it's going to be African teams that are going to be among the best in the world.

Football is a gift. It's given you so much, both on and off the field. What do you hope this sport will give to young African boys and girls?

Umenyiora: Exactly what it's given me, and even more. I thank God for the sport. I know it takes a beating in a lot of instances, and maybe it's deserved in some form or fashion, but from my vantage point, there's really nothing like it.

The opportunities that this game provides to people, whether that's to get an education. If you are African, the ability to get a scholarship... and then now they're paying them in school. Then, on top of that, the opportunity to get to the NFL, which is a rare thing.

But overall, the values that it teaches — the discipline, the sacrifice, the hunger — there's really no other sport like it to me. The teamwork, the camaraderie — I wish everybody could have those experiences. For me, it's just a matter of trying to provide as much of that as possible to as many African people as possible.

Okay, to wrap up, I've got a quick game for us. This or That. Just go with your gut.
Start, bench, cut: Jollof Rice, rice and stew, pounded yam and egusi?

Umenyiora: Start plantain, bench fried yam, and I'm going to cut akara.

Puff puff or meat pie?

Umenyiora: Oooh, I'm sorry I can't choose.

You have to pick.

Umenyiora: Meat pie! But puff puff, oh my gosh.

Afrobeats or Amapiano?

Umenyiora: Afrobeats

Name your top three Afrobeats artists?

Umenyiora: Wizkid, Asake, and Tems she's incredible.

What Afrobeats song has been on repeat for you?

Umenyiora: "Money Constant” by DJ Maphorisa, DJ Tunez, Wizkid, and Mavo

Editor’s Note: By Way of Africa is a series committed to highlighting the talent and stories from the African continent and its diaspora. African stories are worth telling, and the culture—all of the languages, tribes, and traditions—is worth celebrating. Embedded in these narratives is a profound testament to the diligence, discipline, and work ethic deeply ingrained in African heritage. Whether born on the continent or dispersed across the globe, the contributions of these stories to society resound uniquely, by way of Africa.

item.title: Xavier McKinney says he was fined for criticizing officials after Packers-Lions game
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: After Sunday's loss to the Lions, Packers safety Xavier McKinney had some things to say about the officiating.
item.content:encoded:
After Sunday's loss to the Lions, Packers safety Xavier McKinney had some things to say about the officiating. And he knew he was inviting a fine.

After Thursday night's win over the Panthers, McKinney confirmed that he was fined.

Via Rob Demovsky of ESPN, McKinney didn't disclose the specific amount. He did say it wasn't less than the minimum of $25,000.

"I make enough money so I’ll be OK," McKinney said.

McKinney said it was worth it to support the team.

Meanwhile, it's unknown whether Raiders minority owner Tom Brady was fined for his criticism of the officials during that same game.

Through it all, the NFL essentially has conceded that referee Alex Moore's crew didn't meet the standard, by flexing Moore's crew out of Sunday night's game between the Eagles and Commanders.

item.title: David Bailey doubtful, Breece Hall questionable for Sunday vs. Raiders

item.content:encoded:
The Jets are unlikely to have one of their top young defensive players when they host the Raiders on Sunday.

Head coach Aaron Glenn told reporters in his Friday press conference that edge rusher David Bailey will not practice on Friday and is doubtful for the game.

Bailey is dealing with a groin injury and has not practiced this week.

The No. 2 overall pick of this year’s draft, Bailey has registered 5.5 sacks, seven tackles for loss, and nine QB hits so far this season. He also has three forced fumbles.

Running back Breece Hall (quad) will once again be limited in practice on Friday and is questionable for Sunday’s game. He has been limited in practice all week.

Offensive lineman Dylan Parham (knee) will also be questionable.

Defensive lineman T’Vondre Sweat (knee) has been ruled out.

item.title: Panthers fire defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: At 3-4, Carolina shakes up the defensive side of the ball.
item.content:encoded:
Panthers owner David Tepper had big expectations for his team in 2026. With a 3-4 record after seven games, the team is making some big changes.

The Panthers have announced the terminations of defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero and defensive passing game coordinator Jonathan Cooley.

Moving forward, defensive line coach Todd Wash will serve as defensive coordinator and call the defensive plays.

Outside linebackers coach/run game specialist AC Carter will also coach the defensive line, and secondary coach Renaldo Hill will continue to oversee the defensive backs.

Evero, 45, had worked for the Panthers since 2023, arriving as a member of Frank Reich's staff. Evero remained in place after the hiring of Dave Canales in 2024.

In 2022, Evero was the defensive coordinator of the Broncos. His first job as an NFL position coach came in 2017, when Rams coach Sean McVay hired Evero to serve as safeties coach on McVay's initial staff. Evero was secondary coach and passing game coordinator for the Rams in 2021, which resulted in a Super Bowl win.

Through it all, the Panthers remain tied for first place with the Falcons in the NFC South.

item.title: Christian Watson cleared, on his way back to Lambeau from hospital
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: The Packers wide receiver was injured in the second quarter.
item.content:encoded:
Packers wide receiver Christian Watson was cleared at a local hospital and is on his way back to Lambeau Field, Kaylee Hartung of Amazon Prime reports. The Packers still list Watson as questionable to return.

Watson was injured on a 53-yard reception with 9:11 remaining in the first half. He appeared on land on the ball as Panthers cornerback Will Lee landed on him.

Watson was sent in an ambulance to a hospital for further evaluation, with the sternoclavicular joint as a possible concern.

The Packers initially listed Watson as questionable to return with a chest injury.

He has six catches for 100 yards tonight, giving him a career-high 695 receiving yards for the season.

The Panthers have ruled out Lee with a hamstring injury. He was injured on the same play as Watson.

The Packers have ruled out tight end Josh Whyle (concussion).

Packers running back Josh Jacobs scored on a 4-yard reception from Jordan Love with 7:30 remaining in the third quarter to take a 27-10 lead.

UPDATE 10:25 P.M. ET: Watson has returned to the game.

item.title: Ben Johnson is going for it on fourth down even more than Dan Campbell
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Lions head coach Dan Campbell has earned a reputation as one of the NFL's most aggressive coaches on fourth downs, a reputation that he bolstered on Sunday with a surprising fourth down attempt at his own 24-yard line late in the fourth quarter against the Packers.
item.content:encoded:
Lions head coach Dan Campbell has earned a reputation as one of the NFL’s most aggressive coaches on fourth downs, a reputation that he bolstered on Sunday with a surprising fourth down attempt at his own 24-yard line late in the fourth quarter against the Packers. But it's one of Campbell's former assistants who is going for it on fourth down more than any other coach in the NFL.

Bears head coach Ben Johnson has had his team go for it on fourth down 17 times this season, the most in the NFL. Campbell's Lions, on the other hand, have gone for it on fourth down 13 times, tied for the sixth-most in the NFL.

The Lions have punted twice more than the Bears have, while the Bears have attempted five more field goals than the Lions have. The two teams are similar in all three categories of decisions a coach can make on fourth down, but it's noteworthy that it's Johnson who has gone for it the most in the league so far this season.

Before Campbell's surprising decision on Sunday against the Packers, the most controversial fourth down decision of this NFL season may have been the first fourth down decision Johnson made this season, when the Bears went for it on fourth-and-1 from their own 21-yard line against the Panthers in Week 1. Caleb Williams was stopped for no gain, but the Bears still won the game, and afterward Johnson said the call was part of his overall aggressive approach to trying to field the highest-scoring offense in the NFL.

Confidence in their offense is one thing Campbell and Johnson have in common. They'd rather have the game in the hands of their playmakers than on the feet of their kickers.

item.title: New report paints fuller picture of the Troy Aikman, Joe Buck rift
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The inevitable Saturday Night Live skit should be very entertaining.
item.content:encoded:
The inevitable Saturday Night Live skit should be very entertaining. But maybe not as entertaining as the reality.

With the dysfunction between Troy Aikman and Joe Buck continuing to simmer, Andrew Marchand of The Athletic has provided the clearest and most comprehensive details yet as to what happened, in a lengthy article that delves into the nooks and crannies of a 25-year relationship gone sour.

There's a lot there, and it's worth reading the whole thing. For these purposes, here are the facts that seemed to be the most significant.

First, Marchand reports that, before the Week 5 Monday night game in L.A. between the Bills and the Rams, ESPN president Jimmy Pitaro "had a tense one-hour chat" with Aikman. Per the report, Aikman and Pitaro "discussed the rupture" between Aikman and Buck, "and whether there is a future for the duo."

“Could you still work with Joe?” Pitaro asked Aikman. Aikman said he could.

But then came the verbal altercation between Buck and Aikman, with Buck saying to Aikman (per Marchand), "You are not going to fucking talk to me?”

Marchand reports that Aikman believed Buck was hoping to bait Aikman into a backlash that would leave Buck looking like "the good guy."

During their back-and-forth, Buck reportedly said to Aikman, “I’m not the reason you don’t have a contract.” Aikman reportedly suggested that Buck manipulated the constant turnover in the ranks of Monday Night Football producers and directors, telling Buck, "I never thought you'd do it to me." (At some point, Aikman reportedly said more pointedly to Buck, per Dylan Byers of Puck, "You fucked me over!")

Said Buck of the now-former producers and directors, “They got rid of them because you were screaming at them.”

The hard feelings, per Marchand, came from Aikman's perception that Buck and ESPN secretly worked out a new contract "in the early spring" while Aikman was left to wait. That said, Marchand points out that Aikman agreed to leave Fox for ESPN at a time when it wasn't clear whether Buck would be able to follow him to Monday night.

It's unclear when Buck and ESPN specifically did their deal. In mid-April, Buck spoke as if he didn’t have a new contract. An August report from Front Office Sports created the clear impression that neither Buck nor Aikman had a new contract, and that their mutual agency (CAA) possibly would approach the negotiations as a package deal.

And while, as John Ourand of Puck has reported, Aikman's camp at one point sought an increase from $18 million per year to $30 million (thanks to Tom Brady's top-of-market $37.5 million annual pay), Marchand reports that Aikman eventually was willing to take the same 18-percent increase Buck received. ESPN passed.

As Marchand explains it, ESPN has now chosen not to negotiate with Aikman because: (1) it doesn't want to further invest in a relationship gone sour; (2) the network is generally in cost-cutting mode (except when it isn't); and (3) ESPN believes "there is depth in the NFL game-analyst market."

Aikman's side role with the Dolphins, per Marchand, isn't a factor in ESPN's reluctance to proceed. However, Aikman reportedly concedes that he should have told Pitaro about his plan to work for the Dolphins before embarking on the creation of an obvious conflict of interest.

From ESPN's perspective, the negotiations are simply "paused." Marchand reports that ESPN does not have a plan in place for a post-Aikman Monday night booth. Given that ESPN believes "there is depth in the NFL game-analyst market," does it need one? ESPN likely realizes that, if it makes a decision after Super Bowl LXI to move on from Aikman, his seat will be easily filled.

Through it all, Buck and Aikman share close quarters for three hours or more every Monday night. Plenty of people are studying all words uttered and every glimpse of facial expressions and body language in search of evidence of a potential on-air fracas to come.

For now, Aikman sees the handwriting on the wall. He said this week there's a "50-50 chance" he won't be working in TV next year. His public comments about possibly working for the Cowboys (which he now says he regrets) make it clear that he's available and willing to explore a full-time football role with one of the various 32 NFL franchises.

However it plays out, it's unprecedented to have a prime-time network broadcast team in the throes of such public acrimony. On one hand, it tarnishes ESPN's first-ever Super Bowl season. On the other hand, it adds another layer of reality show to the ultimate reality show that is the NFL.

item.title: Report: Bears are close to a deal to stay in Illinois
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: So much for Hammond, Indiana.
item.content:encoded:
The Bears can finally drop the Hammond facade.

After months of claiming that they’re solely focused on building a new stadium in Indiana, the bluff has worked. Via Greg Hinz of Crain's Chicago Business, the Bears are "close to a deal that would keep them in Illinois."

A vote in the Illinois legislature could come as soon as November.

The new venue would "most likely" be built in Arlington Heights, not Chicago. But Illinois is still Illinois. And it's not Indiana.

The new law would allow any municipality (including Chicago) to form an authority that would own and operate the stadium, with no property taxes being paid. Taxpayers would be responsible only for new roads and other infrastructure.

Hinz also reports that recent progress has been fueled by the involvement of Bears minority owner Pat Ryan. Commissioner Roger Goodell also has gotten involved, with majority owner George McCaskey and president/CEO Kevin Warren — who said in August that Hammond, Indiana was the team's "sole focus" — taking a backseat.

It's still not done, but it's the biggest indication yet that the Bears won't be leaving Illinois. Even after repeatedly saying they would.

item.title: Robert Saleh: Titans aren't shopping anyone, but when you're 1-6 teams call you
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Titans head coach Robert Saleh says his team will not hold a fire sale ahead of the trade deadline.
item.content:encoded:
Titans head coach Robert Saleh says his team will not hold a fire sale ahead of the trade deadline. But the offer they got from the Bears for defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons was too good to pass up.

The Bears traded their next two first-round draft picks to the Titans for Simmons, and Saleh said that a team in the Titans' position couldn't realistically have passed that up.

"No one's shopping any of our guys, but like I told our guys, when you don't close out games, and you're standing here at 1-6, teams are going to start fishing," Saleh said. "And eventually a team threw a hook big enough that I don't think any of us could've said no to."

Saleh said he considers Simmons "by far" the best defensive tackle in the NFL and hates to see him go.

"It's tough. Jeff is an elite football player and he's an even better person," Saleh said. "He's an elite leader. I've been outspoken on that. It sucks. Everything about it sucks. Unfortunately, necessary."

Saleh declined to answer when asked what he said to Simmons before he left the Titans' facility for the last time.

"I'll keep that between me and him," Saleh said. "Very, very, very tough conversation."

It was a tough decision for the Titans, but in the long run it may prove to be the correct decision. Those two first-round picks may help the Titans build a winning team, something they don't have now.

item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Watson left Lambeau Field in an ambulance, spent an hour getting checked at the hospital, and then rode in an ambulance back to the stadium and played again.
item.content:encoded:
Packers wide receiver Christian Watson left Lambeau Field in an ambulance on Thursday night after breaking a rib and spitting up blood, but he later returned to the field and said after the game that he never doubted whether he should play through it.

"I was spitting up some blood or something like that, so the doctor said I had to go get a CT," Watson said. "I was trying to beg him to not make me do that. I got a rib, that's all, but the other stuff was good. No internal bleeding, nothing like that."

Watson said he would always play through pain if he possibly could.

"Before I even left I wanted to get back out there," Watson said. "This means everything to me, to be out there on the football field. I've had injuries I was not able to go on the field for, and I've missed significant time due to injuries, so any chance I get to go out there on the football field, I'm going to be out there on the football field."

Watson finished the game with eight catches for 113 yards: Six catches for 100 yards before going to the hospital, and two catches for 13 yards after returning from the hospital.

Watson said his philosophy is simple: "If you can get up, you've got to get up."

item.title: Josh Jacobs denies he was mimicking himself in handcuffs in touchdown celebration
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: After scoring a touchdown on Thursday night, Packers running back Josh Jacobs put his hands behind his back, which many observers interpreted as mimicking himself in handcuffs.
item.content:encoded:
After scoring a touchdown on Thursday night, Packers running back Josh Jacobs put his hands behind his back, which many observers interpreted as mimicking himself in handcuffs. Which would be in poor taste, given that Jacobs is playing only his second game of the season after he was put on paid leave following a no contest plea in connection with a domestic violence accusation brought by his girlfriend.

Jacobs denied that's what he was doing.

Jacobs said the broadcast of Thursday night's game didn't show his full touchdown celebration, which he and teammate Savion Williams planned, and which was inspired by a gospel song.

"They didn't even get the whole celebration," Jacobs said. "Shit, it was fuckin' one second that they just showed me. But anyways, me and Savion came up with the celebration, if they would have seen the whole celebration. Basically, last week, we said the first celebration, when I score, I was gonna thank God, that's what I did last week. Second was going to be 'Break Every Chain.' It's a gospel song. That was gonna be the next celebration. It's a correlation. The media is gonna run with it. They're gonna make it something that it wasn't. But it is what it is."

Although Jacobs' paid leave is over, he remains subject to a potential unpaid suspension for violating the NFL's personal conduct policy.

Panthers quarterback Bryce Young has been on the injury report since hurting his left knee during the team's Week 3 loss to the Browns and he was asked if it was bothering him after Thursday night's game in Green Bay.

The questions came because Young had little luck evading pressure which head coach Dave Canales said "maybe" was related to the knee issue, but Young waved that off when he spoke to reporters.

"Yeah, I’m fine," Young said, via the team's website. "Everyone's dealing with something at this point in the year. It's football. Nothing like that is an excuse; go out there and play the game. I'm blessed to be able to do that. That's all that matters."

The quarterback wasn't helped by the fact that the Panthers were forced to do more shuffling on the offensive line. Right tackle Taylor Moton went on injured reserve this week and left guard Damien Lewis was inactive, which led to Monroe Freeling and Corey Bullock starting up front. Bullock had to leave the game with a quad injury and Jake Curhan entered as the Panthers continued to patch things together on the fly in front of Young.

It didn't work on Thursday and the Panthers will try and come up with something better when they try to snap their losing streak at home against the Broncos in Week 9.

item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: The Packers improved to 5-3 despite a sluggish fourth quarter.
item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers celebrated their World Series with a trip to Lambeau Field. The Packers joined in the celebration with a 27-19 victory over the Panthers.

It was closer than it should have been.

Trey Smack missed an extra point; the Packers turned it over three times, including a fumbled kickoff; and Green Bay let Carolina climb back into it after leading 27-10 midway through the third quarter. It's the same problems the Packers have faced over the past two seasons — poor special teams play and choking big leads.

The Panthers outgained the Packers 109 to 32 in the fourth quarter.

The Packers didn't blow this one, though, moving to 5-3. The Panthers fell to 3-4.

Panthers quarterback Bryce Young threw incomplete on fourth-and-5 at midfield with 2:41 left in their best chance for a comeback.

Packers wide receiver Christian Watson left in an ambulance for a local hospital with 9:11 remaining in the first half. He had his chest injury examined there, and doctors cleared him to return. Watson returned to Lambeau Field in the passenger seat of the ambulance and had a clutch 7-yard reception on third-and-2 with 2:33 left. It allowed the Packers to run down the clock, with Carolina getting the ball back with only 22 seconds left.

Young was sacked six times, including by rookie Dani Dennis-Sutton with four seconds remaining.

Young, who was hit nine times, was 23-of-41 for 209 yards with a touchdown and an interception. Chuba Hubbard had 22 carries for 81 yards and a touchdown and seven catches for 38 yards. Tetairoa McMillan had six catches for 58 yards.

Ryan Fitzgerald made field goals of 39 and 50 yards.

The Packers outgained the Panthers 354 to 258.

Love finished 30-of-41 for 288 yards with three touchdowns and an interception. His touchdowns covered 12 yards to Tucker Kraft, 24 yards to Matthew Golden and 4 yards to Josh Jacobs. Jacobs also scored on a 1-yard run.

Jacobs rushed for 39 yards on 21 carries and caught six passes for 13 yards.

Watson had eight catches for 113 yards and Golden seven for 79.

Packers wide receiver Coleman Owen fumbled the opening kickoff, and Watson lost a fumble in the first half. The Panthers, though, got only a field goal out of the three takeaways.

item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Seahawks hope their trade for Quenton Nelson will have an impact on their entire offense over the rest of the season and it will have an immediate impact on two of his new teammates.
item.content:encoded:
The Seahawks hope their trade for Quenton Nelson will have an impact on their entire offense over the rest of the season and it will have an immediate impact on two of his new teammates.

Anthony Bradford is heading to the bench because the team is moving Grey Zabel from left guard to right guard to allow Nelson to remain in the position he's played for his entire NFL career. On Thursday, Zabel admitted to "a lot of emotions" about the change but said that the prevailing one is that it will allow him to grow as a player.

"At the end of the day, I'll do whatever's best for the team," Zabel said, via the team's website. "Get to learn from an unbelievable player, person, leader, as Q is. And at the end of the day, it's going to be such a growing experience for me, kind of move positions as well as be able to learn from a guy like that. And at the end of the day, just become a better football player."

Picking up the nuances of a different position in a couple of days isn't the easiest of asks, but Zabel will have to do it and he could be there for a while. Nelson's in the final year of his contract and a new deal with the Seahawks will leave the right side as Zabel's domain for quite some time.

item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: In five games played since he emerged from a two-year retirement, Rams defensive tackle Aaron Donald has yet to record a sack.
item.content:encoded:
In five games played since he emerged from a two-year retirement, Rams defensive tackle Aaron Donald has yet to record a sack. During his weekly press conference on Thursday, Donald was asked whether that bothers him.

“No. I didn't come back for individual stats," Donald told reporters. "I would love to have some stats, but I'm here to just play the game. When the plays present themselves, take advantage of it, try to get my plays, but my main focus is trying to find ways to help this team win. That's the goal. I didn't come back to try to earn individual accolades or anything. I did that, accomplished that. It doesn't excite me. The only thing that excites me is winning so I’m just playing a football game, trying to do what I can to help this team. As long as we win, I can build off everything else and get myself better off that.”

The Rams have won only three of seven games, and Donald has yet to play with Myles Garrett. Even though it was the trade that brought Garrett to the Rams that lit the fuse to get Donald to return.

Against the Raiders in Week 7, Donald was on the field for 74 percent of the Rams' defensive snaps. It was his highest rate of the season, and the more he's on the field, the more likely he'll be to get some of those stats he'd love to have — even if winning continues to be the focus.

The Rams should get their fourth win of the season on Sunday, against the 0-6 Chargers. If they don't, the Rams will be 3-5 through eight games and dangerously close to having too many losses to play beyond Week 18.

item.title: Troy Aikman says it was "unfair" for him to back Jerry Jones "into a corner"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: ESPN's Troy Aikman has had plenty to say recently about his uncertain professional future.
item.content:encoded:
ESPN's Troy Aikman has had plenty to say recently about his uncertain professional future. On Thursday, he acknowledged that he may have said too much.

Via Brandon Contes of Awful Announcing, Aikman expressed some regret during a Thursday appearance on 96.7 The Ticket in Dallas regarding comments about potentially working for the Cowboys.

“The last thing that I want is — I was answering a question, and I think it’s really unfair to Jerry that he then has to answer these questions,” Aikman said. “As far as, ‘Hey, would you bring Troy back, or would you have a role for him?’ I mean there’s no real good answer that he can give.”

Aikman said he raised the issue with Jones in Philadelphia on Monday night, where Aikman called the game between the Eagles and the Cowboys.

“We briefly touched on it just because I felt that maybe I backed him into a corner that he didn’t deserve to be backed into," Aikman said. "He didn’t ask for it. And so, we’re clear on that. He totally understood, and yet, he was very complimentary if something like that were to ever take place with the idea that we’re not having those conversations at this time.”

Aikman is in an awkward spot of his own. He senses that ESPN doesn't want to bring him back next year. He pegs his chances of having a job in TV next year at "50-50." Part of his own personal coping mechanism seems to be talking about the fact that he feels his 25-year broadcasting career slipping through his fingers.

Aikman now realizes that, in recently talking about possibly working for the Cowboys, he has created a scenario in which Jones will be asked about Aikman possibly working for the Cowboys. Which happened on Tuesday, given that Jones does two radio spots of his own every week on 105.3 The Fan.

Still, Aikman's latest comments are all part of the dance aimed at potentially laying the foundation for Aikman, who was and by all indications still is working for the Dolphins, potentially joining forces with Jerry in an effort to finally put together a team that can possibly get back to the NFC Championship, for the first time since 1995.

He was injured on a 53-yard reception, with Panthers cornerback Will Lee injuring his hamstring on the same play. Lee needed a cart to get into the X-ray room.

Josh Jacobs scored on a 1-yard touchdown run.

The Packers would lead by more if Trey Smack hadn't missed his first PAT try off the left upright, his eighth missed kick of the season. Green Bay also lost two fumbles.

Packers wide receiver Coleman Owen fumbled the opening kickoff, and linebacker Nick Hampton recovered for the Panthers. Carolina gained only 8 yards in the drive before Ryan Fitzgerald kicked a 39-yard field goal for a 3-0 lead.

Watson fumbled on an 8-yard reception, a fumble forced by safety Nick Scott and recovered by Bobby Okereke. The Panthers, though, didn't take advantage of their second takeaway.

item.title: Report: NFL flexes referee Alex Moore's crew out of prime time
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The NFL, for reasons still neither known nor apparent, opted not to flex the game between the 2-5 Eagles and 1-4-1 Commanders out of prime time, despite multiple other compelling Sunday afternoon games.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL, for reasons still neither known nor apparent, opted not to flex the game between the 2-5 Eagles and 1-4-1 Commanders out of prime time, despite multiple other compelling Sunday afternoon games.

The league did, however, flex the officiating crew out of the Sunday night game.

Via Football Zebras, Alex Moore's crew has been moved from Eagles-Commanders to Patriots-Dolphins. Shawn Hochuli's crew will work the Sunday night game.

The report, citing unnamed officiating sources, says that the change is "more about optics rather than a disciplinary action."

Whatever the precise reason, it seems to be a reaction to the various bad calls Moore's crew made in the Week 7 game between the Packers and Lions, including two questionable roughing the passer calls on the Packers and a phantom illegal hit on a defenseless player by Lions linebacker Derrick Barnes.

The optics-driven reason is simple. Moving Moore's crew out of prime time, and relegating them to a secondary 4:25 p.m. ET broadcast on CBS, avoids Mike Tirico and/or Cris Collinsworth mentioning the rough day the crew had in Detroit.

Typically, the various crews are assigned without regard to the broadcast footprint of a given game. In this specific case, it shows that the league would rather avoid further talk about the multiple mistakes that Moore's crew made.

Even though Raiders minority owner Tom Brady did an effective job of highlighting those mistakes to an audience of 24.67 million on Sunday.

item.title: Christian Watson transported to hospital; Will Lee injures hamstring on same play
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: The Packers receiver injured his chest on a 53-yard reception.
item.content:encoded:
Christian Watson caught a 53-yard bomb from Jordan Love with 9:11 remaining in the second quarter.

The Packers wide receiver appeared to land on the ball before Panthers rookie cornerback Will Lee landed on him. Both players remained on the ground after the play.

Watson was holding his chest, and Lee was writhing in pain while grabbing his left hamstring.

Lee needed a cart from the sideline to get to the training room, as he was unable to put weight on his leg. Watson walked to the training room, but since was transported via ambulance to a local hospital for precautionary reasons.

The Packers initially listed Watson as questionable to return with a chest injury.

He has six catches for 100 yards tonight, giving him a career-high 695 receiving yards for the season.

The Packers converted Watson's big catch into a touchdown on Josh Jacobs' 1-yard touchdown run. Green Bay leads 13-10.

The Panthers list Lee as doubtful to return with a hamstring injury.

Chau Smith-Wade replaced Lee, who is the fourth cornerback the Panthers have lost. Jaycee Horn, Mike Jackson and Akayleb Evans are on injured reserve.

item.title: Bears announce trade for DT Jeffery Simmons
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: It was a very big day for the Chicago Bears; they added one of the best defensive tackles in the league, and they're reportedly closing in on a deal to stay in Illinois.
item.content:encoded:
It was a very big day for the Chicago Bears; they added one of the best defensive tackles in the league, and they're reportedly closing in on a deal to stay in Illinois.

The Bears have now officially announced the arrival of Jeffery Simmons. The Bears will send to the Titans a 2027 first-round selection, a 2028 first-round selection, and a 2027 fourth-round selection in exchange for Simmons and a 2028 fifth-round selection

"We are excited to welcome Jeffery Simmons and his family to Chicago," General Manager Ryan Poles said in a team-issued release. "We extend our gratitude to the Tennessee Titans and Mike Borgonzi for their partnership and collaboration throughout this process. We are fortunate to have the opportunity to add a player, and a human, like Jeffery to our team, and we look forward to Jeffery's leadership and command as we continue to work toward sustained success."

Bears coach Ben Johnson expressed his endorsement of the move, too.

"Jeffery is one of the most respected players in the National Football League," Johnson said. "Jeffery has proven to be one of the most impactful run defenders and disruptive pass-rushers in the NFL, and yet, through his leadership, Jeffery will have the opportunity to create a positive impact across our entire team. We look forward to the work ahead."

The move shows that the Bears are ready to make a run at a Super Bowl berth — 20 years after their last NFC Championship and 41 years after their only Super Bowl win.

item.title: CeeDee Lamb on Cardinals' dominance over Cowboys: It's crazy
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: The Cardinals, no matter how bad they have been, have had the Cowboys' number.
item.content:encoded:
The Cardinals, no matter how bad they have been, have had the Cowboys' number. Arizona has won four in a row against the Cowboys and eight of the past nine.

In 2025, the Cardinals beat the Cowboys 27-17 at AT&T Stadium before losing their final nine. Jacoby Brissett is 3-16 in his two seasons in Arizona, including the win over the Cowboys.

Dallas' last win over the Cardinals came on Sept. 25, 2017, in Glendale, a 28-17 win.

"Yeah, it’s just crazy," wide receiver CeeDee Lamb said of the Cardinals' dominance over the Cowboys, via Patrik Walker of the team website. "[We were] being very, very relaxed, and they punched us in the mouth every single time. They've always had more energy. They were more excited, regardless of if it was a 12 o'clock, Sunday night or Monday night.

"We've played them in primetime. They beat us there. So, we need to treat them as if they are a Super Bowl-contending team, which they may be. You know what I'm saying? Hats off to them in their prep, and we just got to go match them, if not overpower that."

The Cardinals are 4-0 at AT&T Stadium, which is where Sunday's game is being played. Two of those wins came with quarterback Kyler Murray as the starter. Murray is 9-0 in his career at the stadium in high school, college and the NFL.

item.title: Mike Macdonald on Anthony Bradford losing starting job: "It's not an easy situation"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: One of the most basic realities of the NFL trade market is that, when a team adds a key player during a given season, someone will be taking a seat.
item.content:encoded:
One of the most basic realities of the NFL trade market is that, when a team adds a key player during a given season, someone will be taking a seat.

In Seattle, the "someone" who will be leaving the starting lineup after the arrival of guard Quenton Nelson is Anthony Bradford. With Nelson taking over at left guard and 2025 first-rounder Grey Zabel moving to right guard, former starting right guard Anthony Bradford will move to the bench.

“It's not an easy situation," coach Mike Macdonald told reporters on Thursday. "I thought Anthony played good football for us, and he has, and he's earned a significant role on our team, a starting-level role. It's one of those ‘through not around’ type of things with AB that is not easy.

"There’s no way to sugarcoat it, and he believes this when we say this, how much we love him. The guys love him in the locker room. He's a fantastic teammate. We don't expect him to be jumping over joy in this situation because that's not realistic, but he's going to be a great teammate and he's going to stay ready.

"We know how this league works. You're a play away from him playing every play again. It's not an easy situation, but he's a tough cookie, and the guys will have his back as well and we're behind him as well, but it's not easy.”

Making it even less easy for Bradford is the fact that the fourth-round pick in 2023 is in a contract year. And it becomes much harder to earn a new contract, in Seattle or elsewhere, if Bradford isn't playing.

The fact that the Seahawks traded for Nelson during Bradford's contract year is a fairly clear sign that the Seahawks are ready to move on.

Bradford has 44 regular-season appearances and 40 regular-season starts. He started all three postseason games in 2025, including Super Bowl LX.

item.title: Cowboys-Eagles' audience blows out World Series Game 3
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: There once was a time when the mere thought of competing with the World Series made the NFL hide under the bed.
item.content:encoded:
There once was a time when the mere thought of competing with the World Series made the NFL hide under the bed. Nowadays, regular-season football is the monster lurking under the World Series' futon.

When ESPN announced the numbers for the Week 7 Cowboys-Eagles game (18.8 million), Fox had yet to disclose the viewership for Game 3 of the World Series between (Googles it) Tampa Bay and Milwaukee. And for good reason.

Via Manny Soloway of Awful Announcing, the baseball game averaged 8.33 million viewers. That made it the fourth-least-watched World Series game ever, behind only Game 3 in 2023, Game 4 in 2023, and Game 3 in 2020.

In the 1970s, the NFL moved Monday Night Football to Thursday, in order to avoid competing with the World Series. Prior to 2010, the NFL avoided playing on Sunday nights, in order to avoid competing with the World Series.

Now, baseball should endeavor to play World Series games when NFL games aren't being played. Which means Tuesday night, Wednesday night, Friday night, and Saturday night.

Until the NFL starts playing on Tuesday night and Wednesday night. Which seems inevitable.
